The declaration, And He is the All-M ighty, the All-W ise reinforces and elucidates this concept, signifying that all forms of honor exclusively belong to Him, untouched by any

form of disgrace. This stems from the understanding that disgrace merely represents a lack of honor, and an entity embodying complete honor cannot be imagined as deficient in it. Furthermore, all forms of wisdom are

His, precluding any association with ignorance, for ignorance is simply the lack of wisdom, and it has been established that He is devoid of any deficiency in wisdom.

Given that neither disgrace nor ignorance can exist within His divine realm, God is inherently free from any traits of inadequacy, any qualities warranting censure or disapproval, or any instances of negativity. In contrast, the essence of a disbeliever is marked by disgrace and ignorance. As

such, traits of deficiency are fundamental to their nature, positioning the disbeliever as a manifestation of negativity.

Contrary to the disbeliever, the believer, despite their inherent def ciencies and ignorance, is safeguarded under God’s protection. God has

bestowed upon them His honor and guided them out of ignorance with His spirit, as evidenced by His words: And God is the ally of the believers

(3:68), And for God is the honor, and for His M essenger, and for the believers (63:8), and Those are the ones whom God has written faith in their hearts

and strengthened them with a spirit from Him (58:22).

(16:61) Were Allah to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave any creature (dābba) upon it. But He

respites them until a specified time; so when their time comes they shall not defer it by a single hour nor shall they advance it.

The pronoun “it” refers to the earth, a detail implicitly understood through the mention of “mankind,” making an explicit reference to “on the earth” unnecessary.

It’s a plausible explanation that, within this context, dābba specif cally denotes humans, given that humans are indeed moving creatures.

Therefore, the verse conveys the notion: “Should God choose to exact punishment on people for their injustices— to the extent that every perpetrator of injustice is penalized—then no human being would be left

walking the earth. This scenario would unfold as wrongdoers would be eradicated due to their injustices, and the virtuous, including prophets and impeccable saints, would never come into existence, as their forebears would have been annihilated.”

Nevertheless, commentators, acknowledging the broad scope of the term dābba, interpret it to encompass all living beings, both humans and animals. From their perspective, the verse suggests: “Should God decide to penalize the oppressors for their wrongdoings, He would annihilate all human beings along with animals.” This interpretation raises the question of why animals, innocent of any wrongdoing, should suffer destruction due to human injustice, suggesting that their demise would be a collateral consequence of the injustice of humans.

A compelling response to this objection, as refined from suggestions by some scholars, posits that the eradication of one generation of humans precludes the birth of subsequent generations, including prophets. The extinction of humanity from the earth would inevitably lead to the demise of other species as well, given that their existence is intertwined with human survival and welfare. This concept is supported by the verse: He created for you all that is on the earth (2:29), (indicating that other creatures’ existence serves human needs and purposes.)

Certainly, alternative interpretations have been suggested to address the critique concerning the broad application of the term “creature” in the verse. However, these interpretations do not substantially enhance the understanding, so for a deeper analysis, readers are encouraged to consult detailed commentaries. We will not elaborate on these alternatives further in this discussion.

Some commentators have utilized this verse to contend that prophets are fallible, interpreting the text’s implication that if God were to annihilate humans for their injustices, no one would survive on earth, as suggesting that prophets too commit injustices. However, this interpretation misreads the verse’s intent. The verse simply states that should God decide

to obliterate humanity for its injustices, the entire human race would face extinction. This does not infer that every individual would be punished for their personal wrongdoing. It’s plausible that the majority might be eradicated due to their own injustices, while a minority could be lost in the fallout of their community’s destruction. Thus, the verse does not suggest that every person, including prophets and those deemed infallible, is guilty of injustice.

In response, it has been argued that the term “mankind” in the verse specifically targets the oppressors within humanity, as indicated by the phrase “for their wrongdoing.” Therefore, this does not encompass the Infallibles in any way.

Others might respond that “wrongdoing” here is broader including any form of disobedience, defined as actions that diverge from the directives of the Almighty. This explanation could extend to actions that are less preferable, contrary to advisory commands, and might apply to prophets as well.

This perspective is supported by the instance of Adam and his wife, who acknowledged, Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:23). Similar errors are attributed to other prophets, leading to the adage, “The good deeds of the righteous are considered faults for those who are close to God” (ḥasanāt al-abrār sayyiʾāt al-muqarrabīn). This suggests that actions deemed virtuous for the righteous may be viewed as shortcomings for those nearer

to God. Thus, the usage of ‘injustice’ in the verse being discussed doesn’t necessarily classify prophets as sinners, in the sense of committing acts of disobedience against God’s commands.

Another group of commentators suggests that the total annihilation mentioned could be exemplified by an act such as God withholding rain.

In such a scenario, it’s clear that both the righteous and the wicked would suffer alike, illustrating the principle that when divine retribution is meted out, it doesn’t distinguish between the virtuous and the sinful—much like “fire consumes both the wet and the dry.” Yet, this form of punishment represents a tribulation and hardship for God’s adversaries, whereas for the faithful, it serves as a trial and an opportunity to augment their divine reward.

However, each of these three explanations presents its own set of lim itations.

The first explanation is problematic because if “mankind” is interpreted to exclusively denote oppressors, logically, only they would face

destruction, as some interpretations have indeed suggested. This then raises the question of why the infallibles would be subject to destruction.

Furthermore, this interpretation does not account for why other creatures would also be destroyed, leaving the assertion that no creature would remain on earth unaddressed.

The second explanation does not hold up well because the verses in question specifically address injustice in the form of polytheism and violations of God’s commands. Expanding the definition of ‘injustice’ to

include actions that are less preferable introduces an interpretation that seems disconnected from the verse’s immediate context. This is particularly evident in the phrase, But He respites them until a specified time, which suggests a looming threat and is incongruous with a broader understanding of “injustice.” Regarding the third explanation, it lacks direct support from the text itself. The idea that divine punishment, like withholding rain, afiects both the righteous and the wicked alike, serving as a calamity for the former and a test for the latter, is not explicitly grounded in the verse’s wording.

But He respites them until a specified time; so when their time comes they shall not defer it by a single hour nor shall they advance it—This verse presents evidence for a contingent matter, with the initial conditional clause suggesting this context. It implies that their reckoning is not rushed but is deferred to an appointed time or a predetermined duration. This appointed time is understood differently for individuals, communities, and humanity at large: for individuals, it is their demise; for communities, their extinction; and for all humanity, the sounding of the trumpet signaling the Day of Resurrection. The Qur’an addresses these meanings of the

appointed time in various verses. For instance, it states: though there are some of you who die earlier—and that you may complete a specified term

(40:67), and elsewhere: And for every nation is a term; when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour nor can they advance it (7:34), and in another verse: And if it were not for a word that went forth from your Lord, judgment would have been rendered between them at once, and those who have wronged would not have been given respite (42:14).

(16:62) They attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues assert the lie that the best reward will be theirs.

Undoubtedly, the Fire shall be their lot and they will be foremost.

This verse revisits the matter of polytheists assigning daughters to God the Almighty while preferring sons for themselves. It explains: Their act of attributing daughters to God stemmed from their aversion to having daughters themselves, whereas they attributed sons to themselves due to their preference and afiection for having sons.

Therefore, the statement, They attribute to Allah what they dislike is specifically about daughters. The following part, and their tongues assert the lie, implies they are spreading falsehoods with their claim that the best rewards await them, implying that those who have sons will receive favorable outcomes. Some interpret “the best reward” as referring to Paradise,

under the assumption of the resurrection and the Day of Judgment being real and the prophets’ words being truthful. This notion aligns with the sentiment in the verse: And if W e let him taste mercy from Us after some adversity has touched him, he will surely say, “This is due to me, and I do not think the Hour will occur; and if I am returned to my Lord, indeed, for me there will be with Him the best” (42:50). This interpretation would hold merit if not for the concluding remarks of the next verse, which we will explore further.

Undoubtedly, the Fire shall be their lot and they will be foremost (mufraṭūn)— This indicates that their fate is sealed to enter the Fire. The term mufraṭ suggests someone who advances or leads; similarly, ifrāṭ implies an excess in hastening, whereas tafrīṭ represents a lack thereof.

The word faraṭ describes a person who moves ahead of a group to arrange necessities like water and shelter. The expression “he sent him ahead” conveys the action of sending someone forward in advance.

The fabrication and their erroneous belief that they can assign to God what is undesirable to them, while securing for themselves what they covet, essentially amounts to presuming they can precede or outpace God Almighty. In response, God clarifies the falsehood of their assumption and the consequence of their deceit, which is the inevitable descent into the Fire. This is encapsulated in the declaration: Undoubtedly, the Fire shall be their lot...

(16:63) By Allah, indeed We sent to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds attractive to them. So he is their ally today, and they will have painful punishment

The context suggests that “today” refers to the day of this verse’s revelation, and “Satan being their ally” means their collective adherence to

misguidance during the time of revelation. The “promised punishment” is understood to be the punishment of the Day of Judgment, as is apparent in most verses that mention punishment.

The meaning is as follows: “By God, indeed We dispatched Our messengers to nations before you, such as the Jews, Christians, and Magians,

and to those not yet extinct like the people of ‘Ad and Thamud. Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them, leading them to follow him and turn away from Our messengers. Thus, he is their guardian today, and they are united in misguidance. And for them, on the Day of Judgment, is a painful punishment.”

Al-Zamakhsharī, based on this reading, has suggested that the pronoun in “their ally” refers to the Quraysh, and the meaning is that Satan adorned the evil deeds of past nations and is today the guardian and protector of the Quraysh. However, the difference in pronouns weakens this possibility.

It is also possible that “nations” refers to extinct past nations, and then the guardianship and leadership of Satan for those nations would be in the realm of Barzakh (the intermediary state after death), where they suffer painful punishment.

Some have said that “today” refers to the entire period of worldly life, and this period is the time of Satan’s guardianship, while the Day of Judgment is the day of punishment.

Others have said that “today” refers to the Day of Judgment, where Satan will have guardianship over them, and it is there that they will have painful punishment. Still, others have said that “today” refers to the day when Satan adorns their deeds, and this expression is a narrative of the past.

However, the first reading seems most appropriate, followed by the second and then the third.

(16:64) We did not send down the Book to you except that you may clarify for them what they differ about, and as a guidance and mercy for a people who have faith.

The pronoun “for them” refers to the polytheists, specifically addressing their disputes over true faith and righteous deeds. The aim of this

clarification is to conclusively present the truth, efiectively completing the argument against them. This reading is supported by the distinction made between the matters of the believers and those of the polytheists, with the believers being mentioned separately as recipients of guidance and mercy, as it is said: and as a guidance and mercy for a people who have faith.

Thus, the essence of the verse is: “The revelation given to you was meant to shed light on the disputes concerning true knowledge and divine commandments. Its purpose was not only to finalize the argument against the disputants but also to act as a beacon of guidance and a blessing of mercy for the believers. Through this revelation, God has laid out His final argument to the disputants, while simultaneously guiding the believers towards the truth and enveloping them in His mercy, as they embrace

and follow this truth.”

Examining Narrations

There are a number of narrations which explain the phrase “people of the Reminder” (ahl al-dhikr) in the verse: So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know has been explained as referring to the Prophet’s Household.

(1) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī narrates via his chain of narrators from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Kathīr, it is narrated that he said to Imam al-Ṣādiq, “What is meant by the verse, So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know?” He replied, “The reminder is Muḥammad, and we are his people, from whom they should ask...”

Author’s comment: This narration refers to the verse: Indeed, God has sent down to you a reminder, a messenger (65:11), and there are many narrations regarding its meaning.

(2) In Tafsīr al-Burhān, from al-Barqī, and he with his chain from Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd Abī al-Daylamī from Abī ʿAbd Allāh, it is narrated that he was asked, “What is meant by the verse, So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know?” He replied, “The reminder is the Qur’an, and the family of Muḥammad are the people of the reminder, whom God has commanded people to ask.” It is evident that God never commands people to ask the ignorant, and He Himself has called the Qur’an the reminder and said: (We have sent down the reminder to you so that you may clarify for the people that which has been sent down to them, so that they may reflect (16:44) and also said: Indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people, and soon you will be questioned (43:44).

Author’s comment: The Imam’s argument is to establish that the Prophet’s Household are the people of the reminder, and that the reminder is the Qur’an, and its people are they, as they are the community of the messenger of God. The two verses he quoted at the end of his speech are for corroborating this meaning, as has been explicitly stated in other narrations and there are other narrations regarding this meaning as well.

(3) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, from Muḥammad b. Muslim from Imam al-Bāqir, it is narrated that he said: “I asked the Imam about the people who are with us, they think that the people of the reminder in the verse, So ask the people of the reminder... are the Jews and Christians. The Imam replied: ‘If they are the ones, they would call you to their religion and would never tell you the truth, which is the validity of Islam.’ Then he pointed to his chest and said: ‘We are the people of the reminder, and we are the ones from whom people should ask.’ Then he added: ‘The reminder is the Qur’an.’”

Author’s comment: A similar explanation has been narrated from Imam al-Riḍā in the assembly of the ʿAbbāsid Caliph al-Maʾmūn.

As previously mentioned, the address in the verse, as the context suggests, is to the polytheists, the idolaters who were plotting against the

prophethood of the Messenger of God. They were commanded to ask the “people of the Reminder,” who are the People of the Book, specifically the Jews, whether God has sent any human messenger to whom He revealed His word. It is evident that since the polytheists did not accept the Prophet himself, it would be meaningless for the Qur’an to tell them to ask the people of the Reminder, as they did not even accept the Qur’an, let alone its people. Thus, we must conclude that the people of the Reminder in the specific context of the verse refers to the People of the Book, especially the Jews.

However, if we disregard the specific context of the verse and take it on its own, then it invokes a general rule that the ignorant, the respondent, and the subject of the response are all general. Any ignorant person who does not know something should ask someone knowledgeable about it.

Therefore, “if you do not know” encompasses all true knowledge, and it is addressed to anyone who might not know something about the knowledge, and the one they are commanded to ask are anyone who is knowledgeable about it. And the epitome of the kind of knowledge with which this

verse is concerned is the Household of the Messenger of God. Because if “the Reminder” refers to the Messenger of God, as in the verse of Sūrah al-Ṭalāq, then surely “the people of the Reminder” will be his family. And if “the Reminder” refers to the noble Qur’an, as in the verse of Sūrah alZukhruf, then in that case, the Qur’an is the remembrance of the M essenger of God and his people—the infallible Imams or the righteous from his people—and he and his people are “the people of the Reminder.” They are the ones whom people are commanded to ask, and the Messenger of God also paired them with the Qur’an in the Tradition of Thaqalayn and commanded people to hold onto both, saying: “They will never separate until they return to me at the Pool...”

One piece of evidence that the words of the Imams in explaining “the people of the Reminder” as the Prophet’s Household, disregarding the specific context of the verse, is that in the narrations, there is no mention of the specific context.

From the above, the invalidity of some objections raised against the aforementioned narrations becomes clear.

One objection is that if “the Reminder” refers to the Messenger of God and “the People of the Reminder” refers to his family, the polytheists did not accept the Prophet to say anything about his family. And in al-Durr al-M anthūr, it is stated that Ibn M ardawayh narrated from Jābir that he said: “The Messenger of God said: ‘It is not appropriate for a scholar to seal his knowledge with silence, nor is it appropriate for the ignorant to remain silent and not ask the knowledgeable, for God Almighty has said:

So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know, so it is incumbent upon every believer to know whether the action he is performing is guided or against guidance.’”

(4) In Tafsīr Al-Qummī, concerning the verse, (Did those who plotted evil deeds then feel secure … unexpectedly (16:45), it is narrated

from the Imam: “When they go for earning and trade, suddenly the punishment seizes them in that state and regarding Or that He might seize them during their movements, he said it means He seizes them while they are awake.”

(5) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī from Samāʿah from Imam al-Ṣādiq, it is narrated that he said: “I asked about the meaning of wāṣib in the

phrase, and to Him is the religion perpetually (wāṣiban), and he replied: ‘It means necessarily.’”

(6) And in Maʿānī al-Akhbār with his chain from Ḥannān b. Sudayr from Imam al-Ṣādiq, it is narrated that in the context of a tradition, he said: and for God is the highest description means a description that is without parallel, indescribable, and beyond imagination.

(7) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, it is stated that Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God said in the

interpretation of the verse, Were Allah to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing (16:61): “If God holds me and Jesus son of Mary accountable for our sins”—and in another narration, it is stated as “me and Jesus son of Mary for the crime committed by this thumb and the finger next to it”—“He would indeed punish us and would not be unjust to us.”

Author’s comment: This tradition contradicts the Book of God and the Sunnah of the Messenger, both of which affirm the infallibility of the prophets, and there is no way to interpret this tradition as referring to the omission of a preferable action, as such omission does not incur punishment.
